query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An adaptive, multi-fidelity free-energy integration scheme that employs on‐the‐fly machine-learning corrections can substantially reduce the computational cost of obtaining accurate fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties while retaining the full vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions compared to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD approaches.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental, binary, and multicomponent high‐entropy alloys (HEAs) near the melting point, where both the solid and liquid phases require accurate free-energy evaluation.
generation.intervention: Implement an adaptive free-energy integration protocol that uses a fast, data-driven sampling routine guided by machine-learning corrections, periodically anchored by high-fidelity ab initio calculations to capture regions with high anharmonicity and strong electron–vibration coupling.
generation.conditions: Test at temperatures from approximately 0.8 to 1.2 times the melting temperature (T_m). Begin with elemental and binary systems for calibration and extend to complex, multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
generation.structural_mediator: The adaptive multi-fidelity integration framework acts as the mediator by dynamically concentrating computational efforts on the most challenging regions of the free-energy landscape while using ML to interpolate in less critical regions.
generation.mechanism: The ML model rapidly samples the free-energy landscape, predicting likely low-error regions, and high-fidelity ab initio calculations are selectively conducted where large anharmonic or electron–vibration effects are expected. This coupling reduces overall simulation time while ensuring that the critical contributions to the free energy are accurately captured.
generation.predicted_outcome: Fusion free energies and derived observables (e.g., latent heat and fusion entropy) will be computed with an accuracy comparable to full explicit ab initio MD, but with a speed-up potentially on the order of several magnitudes relative to ab initio MD and significantly faster than TOR-TILD, especially for multicomponent HEAs.
generation.baseline: The current state-of-the-art approaches include full explicit ab initio molecular dynamics free-energy evaluations and TOR-TILD, both of which are either extremely costly or efficient only for simpler systems.
generation.boundary: The method is expected to perform reliably for systems with moderate to high anharmonicity and electron–vibration coupling, specifically within the temperature window near melting (approximately 0.8–1.2 T_m) for elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy alloys. Its performance in systems with extreme or unexpected behavior remains to be validated.
generation.uncertainty: The exact speedup factor and error tolerances are uncertain and likely depend on the system complexity and the quality of the machine-learning training data. There is also uncertainty regarding how well the adaptive corrections will capture highly localized anharmonic or electron-coupled effects compared to explicit MD.

falsification_experiment.design: Apply the adaptive multi-fidelity integration scheme to a set of benchmark systems: first, select well-studied elemental and binary alloys near their fusion conditions; then extend to one or more multicomponent high-entropy alloys. Run parallel simulations using the new method and full explicit ab initio MD (and, optionally, TOR-TILD) to compute phase free energies and associated thermodynamic observables.
measurements: Phase free energies (for both solid and liquid states)
Derived observables such as latent heat and fusion entropy
Total computational time and resource usage
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the free-energy differences or derived observables obtained with the adaptive ML scheme deviate by more than an acceptable threshold (e.g., >5% error) relative to explicit ab initio MD results, or if the computational speed-up is not significantly better (e.g., less than a 10x reduction in cost) compared to TOR-TILD when applied to multicomponent systems.

Machine-learning interatomic potential

In this section, we discuss the results of the development of the interatomic-potential model used to enable the application of MD simulations of dislocation properties in bcc MoNbTaW. We employ the general framework of machine-learning (ML)-based approaches, which have emerged recently as a systematic framework to develop potentials with accuracies near that of the underlying DFT calculations for elemental and multicomponent systems [24] , [44] – [46] . Here, using training data reported previously [24] for elemental, binary, ternary, and quaternary systems in Nb–Ta–Mo–W, we developed a potential for the MoNbTaW RHEA based on the moment tensor potential (MTP) formalism, which has been found to feature an excellent balance between accuracy and computational cost [46] . The basic materials property predictions of the MTP model are provided in Supplementary Table 1 . decision.trend: Early work on fusion properties relied on empirical-potential and first‐principles models that targeted the phase‐transition temperature by simplifying the entropy contributions. Later, explicit ab initio MD free‐energy evaluations were shown to achieve the needed accuracy—in that they retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration couplings—but at a very high computational cost. TOR-TILD then raised throughput for elemental and binary systems using clever thermodynamic integration but began to falter for complex, multicomponent high‐entropy alloys where the cost of fully sampling the free-energy landscape is prohibitive. Thus, the trend has been from simple temperature forecasts toward high-fidelity but computationally intensive methods that struggle to scale with compositional complexity.
decision.unsolved: A method that can cost-effectively compute accurate free energies (including all entropy contributions) for both the solid and liquid phases in multicomponent high‐entropy systems near fusion conditions remains elusive. In particular, efficiently capturing anharmonic effects and electron–vibration coupling without resorting to prohibitively expensive MD simulations is still an unsolved challenge.
decision.lever: an adaptive, multi-fidelity free-energy integration scheme that uses on-the-fly machine-learning corrections
decision.why: By integrating a fast, data-driven sampling routine with periodic high-fidelity ab initio corrections, this method promises to concentrate computational resources on regions where anharmonicity and electron-vibration coupling are most significant. This lever builds on the prior success of TOR-TILD in simpler systems and the high accuracy of explicit ab initio MD—but it introduces an adaptive sampling mechanism that modern machine-learning techniques can enable. As a result, the method is expected to run at speeds orders of magnitude faster than full MD while maintaining free-energy fidelity comparable to explicit approaches. The approach would be benchmarked for elemental and binary systems near 0.8–1.2 times the melting temperature and then extended to multicomponent high-entropy alloys, with decisive falsification occurring if predicted phase free energies or derived observables (e.g., latent heat or fusion entropy) deviate beyond established tolerances relative to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics results.
